This paragraph runs the whole width of the window with no maximum width, so each line holds far too many characters to read comfortably. It is also set in a pale grey on white, which fails the contrast minimum, and it uses a line height of 1.1, which squeezes the lines together. Readers lose their place when they jump back to the start of the next line, and the low contrast makes every word a little harder to see than it should be. We keep adding words here so that the paragraph wraps onto several lines at desktop width and the line length check has real lines to measure, which it will find to be far longer than the comfortable range.

Another paragraph in a slightly different grey and a different size, with a different left margin, so it lines up with nothing above or below it. The spacing values around it are random as well: seven, thirteen, three. None of them sit on a four pixel grid, and none of them repeat anywhere else on the page, which is exactly the kind of drift a spacing scale is meant to stop before it starts. It also keeps going for a while so that the measure check sees several long lines here too.

This whole paragraph is set in capital letters with text transform, which makes a long run of text slow to read because the shapes of the words disappear and every line looks like a solid block.

Sixteen pixels in a serif face with almost no line height, so the descenders of one line touch the ascenders of the next one whenever the text wraps.

Seventeen pixels and semibold in a slightly darker grey than the paragraph before it.

Eleven pixels and a thirty one pixel indent for no reason at all.

Nineteen pixels in a novelty face, because why not add one more family.
